title: Bees and ants do not reason
source_text: Οὐχ ὁρῶν δ᾿ ὁ γεννάδας, ὅσων φιλοσόφων. τὴν πρόνοιαν εἰσαγόντων καὶ διὰ τὰ λογικὰ πάντα ποιεῖν αὐτὴν λεγόντων, συναναιρεῖ τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ αὑτῷ χρήσιμα δόγματα τῇ Χριστιανῶν κατὰ ταῦτα πρὸς φιλοσοφίαν συμφωνίᾳ, οὐδ᾿ ὅση βλάβη κωλυτικὴ γίνεται εὐσεβείας ἐκ τοῦ παραδέξασθαι ὅτι οὐδὲν μυρμήκων ἢ μελισσῶν διαφέρει ὁ ἄνθρωπος παρὰ τῷ θεῷ, φησὶν ὅτι, εἰ διὰ τοῦθ᾿ οἱ ἄνθρωποι διαφέρειν δοκοῦσι τῶν ἀλόγων, ἐπεὶ πόλεις ᾤκησαν καὶ χρῶνται πολιτείᾳ καὶ ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἡγεμονίαις, τοῦτ᾿ οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος ἐστὶ, καὶ γὰρ οἱ μύρμηκες καὶ αἱ μέλισσαι. μελίσσαις γοῦν ἐστιν ἡγεμὼν, ἔστι δ᾿ ἀκολουθία τε καὶ θεραπεία καὶ πόλεμοι καὶ νῖκαι καὶ τῶν ἡττημένων αἱρέσεις καὶ πόλεις καὶ προπόλεις γε καὶ ἔργων διαδοχὴ καὶ δίκαι κατὰ τῶν ἀργῶν τε καὶ πονηρῶν· τοὺς γοῦν κηφῆνας ἀπελαύνουσί τε καὶ κολάζουσιν. οὐδ᾿ ἐν τούτοις δὲ ἑώρακε, τίνι διαφέρει τὰ ἀπὸ λόγου καὶ λογικῆς ἐπιτελούμενα τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἀλόγου φύσεως καὶ κατασκευῆς ψιλῆς γινομένων. ὧν τὴν αἰτίαν οὐδεὶς μὲν ἐνυπάρχων τοῖς ποιοῦσι λόγος ἀναδέχεται (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχουσιν αὐτὸν), ὁ πρεσβύτατος δὲ καὶ υἱὸς μὲν τοῦ θεοῦ πάντων δὲ τῶν ὑποκειμένων βασιλεὺς φύσιν ἄλογον πεποίηκε, βοηθοῦσαν ὡς ἄλογον τοῖς οὐκ ἀξιωθεῖσι λόγου. πόλεις οὖν παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις μετὰ πολλῶν ὑπέστησαν τεχνῶν καὶ διατάξεως νόμων· πολιτεῖαι δὲ καὶ ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἡγεμονίαι ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἤτοι αἳ κυρίως εἰσὶν οὕτως καλούμεναι σπουδαῖαί τινες ἕξεις καὶ ἐνέργειαι. ἢ καὶ αἱ καταχρηστικώτερον οὕτως ὀνομαζόμεναι πρὸς τὴν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐκείνων μίμησιν· ἐκείναις γὰρ ἐνορῶντες οἱ ἐπιτετευγμένως νομοθετήσαντες συνεστήσαντο τὰς ἀρίστας πολιτείας καὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἡγεμονίας. ὧν οὐδὲν ἐν τοῖς ἀλόγοις ἔστιν εὑρεῖν, κἂν ὁ Κέλσος τὰ λογικὰ ὀνόματα καὶ ἐπὶ λογικῶν τεταγμένα, πόλιν καὶ πολιτείας καὶ ἀρχὰς καὶ ἡγεμονίας, ἀναφέρῃ καὶ ἐπὶ μύρμηκας καὶ μελίσσας, ἐφ᾿ οἷς οὐδαμῶς μὲν τοὺς μύρμηκας ἢ τὰς μελίσσας ἀποδεκτέον (οὐ γὰρ σὺν λογισμῷ ποιοῦσι), τὴν θείαν δὲ φύσιν θαυμαστέον, μέχρι τῶν ἀλόγων ἐκτείνασαν τὸ οἱονεὶ πρὸς τὰ λογικὰ μίμημα, τάχα πρὸς δυσωπίαν τῶν λογικῶν, ἵν᾿ ἐνορῶντες μύρμηξιν ἐργατικώτεροι γίνωνται καὶ ταμιευτικώτεροι τῶν ἑαυτοῖς χρησίμων, κατανοοῦντές τε μελίσσας πείθωνται μὲν ἡγεμονίαις διαιρῶνται δὲ τὰ χρήσιμα τῆς πολιτείας ἔργα πρὸς σωτηρίαν τῶν πόλεων.
pass_a_gloss: Not seeing (ὁράω), the noble fellow (γεννάδας, ironic), of how many philosophers (φιλόσοφος), introducing (εἰσάγω) providence (πρόνοια) and saying that it makes all things on account of the rational ones (τὰ λογικά), he destroys together (συναναιρέω), as far as in him (τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ αὑτῷ), the useful doctrines (χρήσιμα δόγματα), with the agreement (συμφωνία) of Christians toward philosophy in these respects; nor how much harm (βλάβη) hindering (κωλυτικός) piety (εὐσέβεια) comes from accepting (παραδέχομαι) that man differs (διαφέρω) in nothing from ants (μύρμηξ) or bees (μέλισσα) with God (παρὰ τῷ θεῷ), he says [Celsus]: 'if on this account men seem to differ from the irrational, since they have dwelt in (οἰκέω) cities and use a constitution (πολιτεία) and offices (ἀρχή) and leaderships (ἡγεμονία), this is nothing to the point (οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος); for also the ants and the bees. Bees at least have a leader (ἡγεμών), and there is following (ἀκολουθία) and service (θεραπεία) and wars (πόλεμος) and victories (νίκη) and takings (αἵρεσις) of the defeated (ἡττάομαι) and cities and fore-cities (πρόπολις) and succession (διαδοχή) of works (ἔργον) and judgments (δίκη) against the idle (ἀργός) and wicked (πονηρός); the drones (κηφήν) at least they drive off (ἀπελαύνω) and punish (κολάζω).' Not in these either has he seen in what the things accomplished from reason (λόγος) and reasoning (λογική) differ from those coming about from irrational nature (ἄλογος φύσις) and bare constitution/equipment (κατασκευὴ ψιλή); of which no reason existing within (ἐνυπάρχω) those doing them accepts (ἀναδέχομαι) the cause (αἰτία) (for they do not even have it), but the most ancient/eldest (πρεσβύτατος), both Son of God (υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ) and King (βασιλεύς) of all subject things (τὰ ὑποκείμενα), made an irrational nature, helping (βοηθέω) as irrational those not deemed worthy (ἀξιόω) of reason. Cities then among men subsisted (ὑφίσταμαι) with many arts and arrangement (διάταξις) of laws; and constitutions and offices and leaderships among men are either those properly (κυρίως) so called, certain virtuous (σπουδαῖος) states (ἕξις) and activities (ἐνέργεια), or those named so more by misuse/loosely (καταχρηστικώτερον) toward the imitation (μίμησις) of those as far as possible. For looking into (ἐνοράω) those, those who legislated (νομοθετέω) successfully (ἐπιτετευγμένως) established (συνίστημι) the best constitutions and the offices and the leaderships. Of which nothing is to be found in the irrational, even if Celsus refers (ἀναφέρω) the rational names (λογικὰ ὀνόματα), assigned (τάσσω) to rational beings — city and constitutions and offices and leaderships — also to ants and bees; for which one must in no way approve (ἀποδεκτέον) the ants or the bees (for they do not act with reasoning, λογισμός), but must marvel at (θαυμαστέον) the divine nature, having extended (ἐκτείνω) as far as the irrational the as-it-were imitation (μίμημα) toward the rational, perhaps toward shaming (δυσωπία) the rational, so that, looking at ants, they may become more industrious (ἐργατικός) and more storing (ταμιευτικός) of things useful to themselves, and, considering (κατανοέω) bees, they may obey (πείθομαι) leaderships and divide the useful works of the commonwealth toward the safety of the cities.
pass_b_english: Our noble friend does not see how many philosophers there are, philosophers who bring in providence and say that it makes all things for the sake of rational beings, whose useful doctrines he is doing away with, as far as he can, along with the agreement of Christians with philosophy on these points. Nor does he see how great a harm, one that hinders piety, comes from accepting that in God’s sight man differs in no way from ants or bees. He says: “If men are thought to differ from the irrational animals because they live in cities and have a constitution, offices and governments, this is nothing to the point; for so do ants and bees. Bees, at any rate, have a leader, and they have a following and service, wars and victories and the capture of the defeated, cities and even outskirts, the handing on of work in turn, and penalties against the idle and the wicked; at any rate they drive away and punish the drones.”

Here too he has not seen how what is accomplished by reason and rational thought differs from what comes about from irrational nature and mere physical make-up. For these latter, no reason dwelling within the creatures that do them is responsible, since they have none; rather, the most ancient Word, who is the Son of God and King of all that is subject to him, has made an irrational nature which, being irrational, comes to the help of those not granted reason.

Cities, then, came into being among men together with many arts and an ordering of laws. And the constitutions, offices and governments among men are either those so called in the proper sense, which are certain virtuous dispositions and activities, or those given these names in a looser sense, because they imitate the former as far as they can. For it was by looking to those that successful lawgivers established the best constitutions, offices and governments.

None of these can be found among irrational creatures, even if Celsus carries over to ants and bees the names that belong to reason and are assigned to rational beings: city, constitutions, offices and governments. For these things we must in no way commend the ants or the bees, since they do not act with reasoning. We must rather marvel at the divine nature, which has extended even to irrational creatures something like an imitation of rational beings, perhaps to put rational beings to shame: so that, looking at ants, they may become more industrious and more careful to store up what is useful to them (Proverbs 6:6–8), and, observing bees, they may obey their governments and share out the useful tasks of the commonwealth for the safety of their cities.

choices.choice: Opening sentence recast: it misplaced 'philosophers' after the clause and used the old-fashioned 'as far as in him lies'; now 'as far as he can', with the agreement destroyed along with the doctrines
Celsus: 'have built cities' -> 'live in cities' (oikeo = dwell)
kataskeue psile: 'mere constitution' -> 'mere physical make-up' (avoids clash with 'constitution' = politeia)
'Son of God' -> 'the Son of God'; 'helps, as an irrational nature can' -> 'being irrational, comes to the help of' (hos alogon); 'not counted worthy' -> 'not granted'

γεννάδας ('noble fellow') is ironic. Celsus's words from εἰ διὰ τοῦθ᾿ to κολάζουσιν are direct speech and are quoted. ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἡγεμονίαι rendered 'offices and governments' throughout chapters 81–83. προπόλεις ('fore-cities, outskirts') may play on πρόπολις, the bees' propolis or hive-glue; rendered 'outskirts'. ἔργων διαδοχή rendered 'the handing on of work in turn' (relays or succession of labours). In the clause ὁ πρεσβύτατος δὲ καὶ υἱὸς μὲν τοῦ θεοῦ the noun λόγος is understood from the preceding 'no reason (λόγος) dwelling within': Origen plays on λόγος as 'reason' in creatures and as the divine 'Word'; 'Word' is supplied in English and capitalised. πρεσβύτατος is not the Pauline πρωτότοκος (Colossians 1:15), so no citation is given for it. The ant clause (more industrious, storing up what is useful) clearly alludes to Proverbs 6:6–8 (the ant gathers food in summer and stores it at harvest); the Septuagint adds lines on the bee (6:8a–c) praising her as industrious, which may lie behind the bee example, but Origen's point there (obeying governments, dividing tasks) is not in that text, so only the ant clause is cited inline. The Stoic distinction between constitutions 'properly so called' (virtuous dispositions) and those so named loosely is reported, not attributed to a named source.
